ogTitle: 10 Popular Restaurants in Songkhla Province 2026 — Eat Like a Local
ogDesc: Kiad Fang stew rice, Hat Yai dim sum, Ko Yo seafood, old-style clay-pot ice cream, and more of Songkhla's best — all in one list with signature dishes and planning tips
intro: Songkhla is a city of great food from morning to midnight — hot stew rice in the old town, generous dim sum in Hat Yai, and fresh seafood by the lagoon on Ko Yo. We've gathered the 10 restaurants locals actually visit and travellers talk about most. Read on to see which spots are worth your time and what to order.

blocks.html:
The charm of Songkhla is its three-culture blend — Thai, Chinese, and Malay — woven seamlessly into every plate. Walk into the old town around Nang Ngam Road and you catch the fragrance of spices from a stew-rice pot, the sound of dim sum steamer lids clinking, and the sight of family shophouses open since the third generation. Shift over to Hat Yai and the mood changes: a city that wakes at five in the morning for dim sum and ba kut teh, then sends you out to Ko Yo for lagoon-view seafood in the evening. Plan the food right and a single trip covers savoury, sweet, and snacks without any overlap.

This list spans legendary institutions and spots that a new generation keeps discovering. Kiad Fang stew rice on Nang Ngam Road has been next to the city for nearly nine decades, and stew rice was once named the provincial signature dish. Tae Hiang Io is the venerable Thai-Chinese Teochew house known for its yam mamuang and sour fish curry. On the Hat Yai side, Chok Dee Tae Tiam is the dim sum and ba kut teh shop with queues forming at dawn; Go Auan Baozi is the original fried bao that has been at it for four decades; and the old-style clay-pot ice cream with salted egg and Milo powder has drawn people to Nang Ngam Road for over seventy years. Each place has a clear signature — read through and map your eating route.

blocks.name: Kiad Fang Stew Rice (Nang Ngam Road)
blocks.area: Nang Ngam Road, Old Town, Mueang Songkhla District, Songkhla
blocks.signature: Pork stew rice (dark spiced broth, crispy pork, optional offal) served with large steamed bao
blocks.descHtml:
Walking the Songkhla old town and want breakfast the way locals have eaten it for generations? Kiad Fang stew rice on Nang Ngam Road is the first name anyone brings up. The shop has been in this old shophouse since 1937, passed down to the third generation of a Hainanese Chinese family. The signature is pork stew rice ladled with a dark broth slow-simmered with aromatics — choose crispy pork, plain pork, or mixed offal — paired with a large steamed bao that has become its own star. The perfect opening meal of any trip.

The heart of the plate is the stew broth: thick enough to coat, lightly salty-sweet, with clear notes of palo spice and aromatic herbs. Reviews say it pours beautifully over hot steamed rice and the sipping is effortless. Crispy pork has crackling skin and tender meat; offal is clean with no off-smell. The pickled vegetables and fresh garlic provided on the side cut through the richness perfectly. The large bao is hand-sized and fluffy; the filling is generous, and the red bean and mung bean versions made from scratch aren't overly sweet — reviewers call it satisfying and worth the price.

Price runs about 100–250 THB per person — fair for the heritage and quality. Open from 07:00 to 14:00; lively and busy, especially on weekends, drawing both Songkhla locals and tourists. The old-town ambiance of the shophouse is intact — eat while watching Sino-Portuguese architecture outside.

The popularity here is no accident: this stew rice was selected as one of the "One Province, One Dish" provincial heritage menu items in 2023, and Google reviews sit at 4.4 stars. Worth knowing: come in the morning, dishes sell out fast especially on weekends, and the shop is closed on Thursdays. For the best bao selection, arrive before noon.
mustOrder: Pork stew rice (crispy pork / mixed offal)
Large steamed bao with pork filling
Steamed bao with red bean / mung bean
blocks.bestFor: First breakfast in Songkhla old town

blocks.name: Tae Hiang Io
blocks.area: Nang Ngam Road, Old Town, Mueang Songkhla District, Songkhla
blocks.signature: Duck palo with fragrant sauce, tofu topped with crab, yam mamuang, sour curry with sea bass and young coconut shoots, fried grey mullet
blocks.descHtml:
Strolling Nang Ngam Road to photograph the street art and looking for a proper lunch or dinner? Tae Hiang Io is the name Songkhla locals reach for first. Open since 1937, that's over 80 years in a two-bay wooden shophouse, serving Thai-Chinese Teochew home-style food that multiple families have been eating since their grandparents' day. Best enjoyed with a group — order many dishes and share.

Tables almost always have duck palo with fragrant sauce — the palo spice is sweet and savoury — and tofu topped with crab, which arrives loaded with crab meat over silky tofu in a thick sauce. For those who like punchy-sour, the yam mamuang (green mango salad) is crisp and sharp, while the sour curry with sea bass and young coconut shoots balances the gentle sweetness of young coconut against a concentrated sour curry base. Fried grey mullet is crispy outside, sweet inside under a heap of golden fried garlic. Reviews consistently praise the fresh ingredients — especially the seafood — and a flavour that has held steady for decades.

Price around 101–250 THB per person — reasonable for the portion and freshness. The setting is an old-style Chinese restaurant: wooden tables, ceiling fans, a warm retro atmosphere. Two sittings daily: 11:30–14:00 and 17:00–20:00. Located at number 85 Nang Ngam Road, across from the Khong Saen Song snack shop.

Worth knowing: lunch time and weekends are very busy — many reviews recommend calling ahead or arriving slightly before opening. No private parking; street parking nearby. Popular dishes like duck palo and crab tofu can sell out, so arrive early if they're on your list.
mustOrder: Sour curry with sea bass and young coconut shoots
blocks.bestFor: First meal in the province — family or group dining
blocks.spice: Medium (yam / sour curry are tart-spicy — adjustable)

blocks.name: Chok Dee Tae Tiam (Dim Sum and Ba Kut Teh)
blocks.cuisine: Chinese (dim sum and ba kut teh)
blocks.signature: Har gow, crab siu mai, ba kut teh, pork spare ribs in red sauce
blocks.descHtml:
When locals talk about the dim sum that defines Hat Yai, Chok Dee Tae Tiam is the shop people grew up with. Open for over twenty-five years on La Mai Song Khrao Road (Khlong Toei) near Daiichi Hotel in the city centre — famous for generous-sized dim sum at friendly prices alongside a hot pot of Chinese herbal ba kut teh. Perfect for a full Chinese-style breakfast spread or a table-filling group order.

Tables almost always feature har gow with plump, springy prawn filling, jumbo-sized crab siu mai, and pork spare ribs in red sauce with a smooth, rounded flavour. But the true showstopper is the ba kut teh: dark broth from soy-braised pork bones and Chinese herbs, cooked with shiitake, enoki, and tofu skin — dip your pa thong ko into the soup and it all comes together. Reviews consistently praise the herbal fragrance, the just-right concentration, and the large generous portions of dim sum. Sweet-tooth diners can finish with salted-egg lava bao — a balanced sweet-salty end.

Dim sum baskets run about 20–25 THB each; a small ba kut teh pot starts around 120 THB for 1–2 people, a large pot about 350 THB for a full table. Average spend in the low hundreds per person. Open in two sittings: morning 06:00–11:30 and evening 17:00–21:00 every day. The vibe is classic old Chinese restaurant — busy and lively, especially in the morning rush — but the kitchen handles the flow quickly.

Worth knowing: weekend mornings are very crowded — arrive before the peak if you don't want to wait. Street parking nearby is limited; watch for red-and-white kerb marks, as enforcement is real in this area. If you're in Hat Yai and want the crowd-tested local staple, this is the spot to add to your list.
mustOrder: Pork spare ribs in red sauce
blocks.bestFor: Chinese-style breakfast with family or friends

blocks.name: Go Auan Baozi (Original Recipe)
blocks.signature: Original fried bao, steamed bao with various fillings, siu mai
blocks.descHtml:
Go Auan Baozi is the legendary fried bao shop that has been a Hat Yai institution for over four decades. The original branch is tucked in Soi Phaduang Withi in the new market area near Emperor Hotel — a shop where Hat Yai locals grew up, from students coming in for a late-afternoon snack to visitors who track it down. The perfect stop for anyone wanting a classic local bite without spending much.

The star is the fried bao: crispy on the outside while still soft inside, with tightly packed filling that isn't greasy. Red roast pork filling is the most popular — the meat is finely chopped and coated in a just-right sauce. Other options include pork mince with salted egg, taro with salted egg, spicy basil chicken, and cream filling. Steamed bao have soft, plump wrappers with generous fillings; there's also fried siu mai, fried wontons, mantou, and cold drinks like iced tea, iced milk tea, and jasmine tea to pair with the food. Reviews repeatedly praise the generous fillings and non-greasy fried bao.

After a renovation the shop became a two-storey building decorated in modern Chinese style — open and airy with several photo spots around the space. Staff are plentiful and service is fast; the wait for food is short. Prices are friendly — fried bao around 22 THB, steamed bao around 18 THB, drinks around 35 THB — most people spend under 100 THB per head. Open from late afternoon to midnight, approximately 14:30–23:30, closed Tuesdays.

Worth knowing: this branch opens in the afternoon and runs late. For morning purchases, visit the Hat Yai Village or PTT branch instead. Weekend evenings get busy. Some reviews note the indoor space can feel a bit warm. Fried bao is best eaten straight from the kitchen while hot — grab and go, or bring them as gifts.
mustOrder: Fried bao with red roast pork
Fried bao with pork mince and salted egg
blocks.spice: Not spicy (except spicy basil chicken filling)

blocks.name: Nam Kiang Din, Ko Yo
blocks.area: Ko Yo, Mueang Songkhla District, Songkhla
blocks.signature: Grilled sweet clams, squid with roe steamed with lime, garlic-fried sand whiting, stir-fried sea catfish with cha-om
blocks.descHtml:
If you're on Ko Yo and want fresh seafood with a view worth remembering, Nam Kiang Din is one of the most talked-about restaurants on the island among both Songkhla locals and visitors. The restaurant sits on a hillside overlooking Songkhla Lake, with a view stretching across Tin Sulanon Bridge and the water on both sides. A setting many visitors say is worth crossing the bridge for. Great for large family groups, friends who want to sit back and catch an evening breeze, or a couple wanting a long sunset dinner.

Regulars order grilled sweet clams with a punchy dipping sauce, squid with roe steamed with lime — reviewers praise the heat-and-sour kick and the roe-filled bites — garlic-fried sand whiting that's crispy outside and sweet inside, and stir-fried sea catfish with cha-om: spicy, fragrant with krachai, perfect over hot rice. Large prawns come in several preparations. The flavour profile leans Southern bold, and most reviews agree the seafood is genuinely fresh.

Price runs about 251–500 THB per head — good-value lake-view seafood. A minor note that appears in many reviews: drinks are priced noticeably higher than average. Evenings and weekends see queues and slower service; for large groups or a scenic table, call ahead to book.

Open daily 10:00–22:00, on Ko Yo island, Tambon Ko Yo, Mueang Songkhla District — a short drive after crossing Tin Sulanon Bridge, with easy parking and capacity for large groups. The reason this restaurant keeps its steady popularity is that it delivers all three things at once: great views, fresh seafood, and comfortable seating — making it the go-to special-occasion meal for anyone passing through Ko Yo.
mustOrder: Squid with roe steamed with lime
blocks.bestFor: Evening seafood dinner with lake views — family or friend group

blocks.name: Lan Ta Chu by Thong Manee Hat Yai
blocks.signature: Lan Ta Chu fried pork knuckle, black-pepper BBQ pork, stir-fried sataw beans with prawns
blocks.descHtml:
If you've heard of the Lan Ta Chu name from Phatthalung and want to try it without the long drive, the Hat Yai by Thong Manee branch is the answer. A fusion steakhouse that blends Western food with Southern Thai dishes — a natural match. Works for families, couples, or a group of friends who want a long table. Multiple zones: indoor, outdoor, and a rooftop — pick your mood. Warm modern décor, seating for over a hundred, parking available, and card payments accepted.

Popular orders include Lan Ta Chu fried pork knuckle — crackling skin with tender meat — black-pepper BBQ pork served flaming with the house sauce, pineapple, potato salad, and garlic bread (choice of beef, chicken, or ostrich), and stir-fried sataw beans with prawns, which captures the Southern character of the restaurant well. Steak fans: the rib-eye gets reviews for being grilled juicy with clear beef flavour. Fresh prawn pad thai has also been singled out as aromatic and well-textured.

Real-customer reviews consistently point to great atmosphere and service, dishes arriving promptly and well-presented. The Southern and local dishes tend to get slightly more praise than the Western dishes. A few reviewers note some pasta dishes come out a touch sweet, and the seafood spaghetti can be quite spicy — mention your spice preference to the staff.

Price runs about 101–250 THB per person, with some premium dishes higher — accessible for a meal with good atmosphere. Located on Sri Phuwanat Road, Kho Hong sub-district, in Hat Yai town. Open daily around 10:00–22:00. A reliable choice for a celebratory or relaxed meal with company.
mustOrder: Lan Ta Chu fried pork knuckle
blocks.bestFor: A meal with good atmosphere — family or friend group
blocks.spice: Spice available in Southern dishes — state your preference

blocks.name: Jae Ni Fish Congee and Wonton Noodles (Rong Si Daeng Branch)
blocks.signature: Sea bass fish congee, clear pork bone broth, large pieces of fresh fish with no fishy smell
blocks.descHtml:
For a morning start in the Songkhla old town with something that has been here for over 60 years, walk straight to Jae Ni Fish Congee at the Rong Si Daeng branch on Nakhon Nok Road, Tambon Bo Yang. The recipe has been passed down to the third generation, and local Songkhla residents stop in so regularly they barely think of it as a choice. The old-era building has been converted into a welcoming spot while keeping the walled neighbourhood atmosphere and the feel of the lagoon district. Finish eating and walk straight to photograph Rong Si Daeng and the lake.

The star of the menu is sea bass fish congee: a clear pork bone broth, naturally sweet from the bones — no MSG required — with large pieces of firm, fresh sea bass that have almost no fishy smell at all. For noodle lovers, the tom yam dry mee sua with sea bass is the most-reviewed dish: pleasantly tart-spicy tossed with soft noodles. The clear broth option has sea bass wonton soup and sea bass sukiyaki. Prices start at just 60 THB — a meal that fills without draining the wallet.

The appeal of Jae Ni is the straightforward honesty of a legendary shop that doesn't need embellishment: good ingredients, steady technique, consistent flavour over decades. Great for a light, clean meal before walking Nakhon Nok–Nang Ngam Road to see the Sino-Portuguese architecture and street art, or as a relaxed end to a trip.

Come during morning-to-late-morning for the freshest fish and a shorter wait. Parking around the old town is limited — if you're staying on Nang Ngam Road, walking is easy. For an authentic old-town Songkhla taste, a bowl from Jae Ni belongs on your list.
mustOrder: Tom yam dry mee sua with sea bass
blocks.bestFor: Morning-to-late-morning in the old town — light fresh fish before a walk along Nakhon Nok–Nang Ngam Road
blocks.zone: Songkhla old town (Nakhon Nok Road, Tambon Bo Yang, Mueang Songkhla District)
blocks.hours: Open daily (Rong Si Daeng branch) approx. 07:00–15:00
blocks.spice: Mild to medium (tom yam style available)

blocks.name: Clay-Pot Ice Cream, Nang Ngam Road
blocks.area: Nang Ngam Road, Songkhla Old Town, Mueang Songkhla District, Songkhla
blocks.signature: Old-style firm-set coconut ice cream scooped from a clay pot, topped with salted egg yolk and Milo powder
blocks.descHtml:
Clay-Pot Ice Cream on Nang Ngam Road is the traditional coconut ice cream shop that has been part of Songkhla old town for over seventy years, standing across from the City Pillar Shrine. A comfortable walk from the old-town gate or the street art along Nang Ngam Road. The shop takes its name from the handmade small clay pots it uses: ice cream is scooped directly from these pretty little fired-clay crocks and served in matching cups. If you're exploring the old town and want a classic, cooling sweet, this is the right spot — whether you're here for photos, traditional desserts, or just keeping the kids happy.

The dish everyone talks about is the "firm-set egg ice cream" — rich, sweet coconut cream ice cream topped with a salted egg yolk and a dusting of Milo powder for 30 THB. It's the signature and everyone orders it. Those who want the full loaded version can try the toppings ice cream with egg and all the extras: steamed mung beans, foi thong, lod chong, and sticky rice, for around 35 THB. The two main flavours are original coconut and lychee. Reviewers love saying the ice cream is genuinely old-recipe sweet and creamy, the mung beans pair perfectly with the coconut, and the fried fish balls alongside work as a savoury contrast.

The atmosphere is casual and classic — vintage shophouse style on Nang Ngam Road, limited indoor seating, good for a drop-in rest after walking. Most cups run 20–35 THB — very light on the wallet for a dessert this storied. Open daily from around 10:00–18:30 with no days off.

The shop has held customers across generations because the old-recipe coconut ice cream is increasingly rare today, and the charm of the clay pots makes it photogenic. It has become the dessert landmark of any Songkhla old-town trip. Worth knowing: busy on weekends and in the late afternoon — seating is limited, so a group might want to come during the quieter mid-afternoon hours.
mustOrder: Loaded toppings ice cream with egg
blocks.bestFor: A cooling sweet break mid-stroll through the old town

blocks.name: Long Oey
blocks.signature: Sea bass with tamarind sauce, crab stir-fried with cha-plu leaves, crispy snakeskin fish tom klong
blocks.descHtml:
Long Oey is a comfortable, air-conditioned Thai restaurant that moved from near Pak Nam Temple to a new location on Niphat Song Khrao Road, same strip as Siam Nakarin, in central Hat Yai. Works well for anyone who wants to sit down with family or friends in the cool, eat Thai food properly, and not feel rushed. The décor is warm and inviting with easy parking — the name that comes to mind for Hat Yai locals when they think of a solid Thai meal in town.

Popular orders include sea bass with tamarind sauce — the fish is sliced into bite-sized pieces and the sauce gets consistent praise for its deep, rounded flavour. Another favourite is crab stir-fried with cha-plu leaves: bold, fragrant, and generously loaded with crab. Crispy snakeskin fish tom klong is pleasantly sour with a decent ratio of fish. Those who want dessert can finish with fried ice cream and fried banana, both called out in reviews as standout.

Multiple reviewers agree the food is genuinely good, but the prices are on the higher side — a multi-dish order for a group can reach into the thousands, and some feel the portion-to-price ratio could be more generous. Sharing across the table helps the value. Price runs about 200–400 THB per head depending on what you order.

Open evenings from 17:00 onward — an evening meal destination. Service is attentive overall; a few reviewers mention staff attention can feel a little intense at times, but most are happy with both the food and the setting. Worth knowing: prices run higher than average — factor that in — and if you're coming on a weekend evening, calling ahead for a table is a good idea.
blocks.bestFor: Dinner with Thai dishes shared across a large group

blocks.name: Nai Roo
blocks.signature: Garlic-pepper fried pork, fried fish, spicy seafood stir-fry
blocks.descHtml:
Nai Roo is a venerable Thai-Chinese restaurant that has been part of Hat Yai for over 40 years, tucked in a narrow lane off Niphat Uthit 3 Road, Soi 1, next to Kim Yong Market — which is why regulars call it "the shop in the lane." You have to walk a short way into the alley to find it. A classic, no-frills shophouse that both Hat Yai locals and visiting food lovers know well. Best enjoyed by a family or friend group who wants to order multiple dishes and share.

Almost every table orders garlic-pepper fried pork — fragrant with crispy fried garlic — fried pompano with garlic, a large fish with sweet flesh under a mound of golden garlic, and "Ai Khlang Thale Hot" — a spicy mixed seafood stir-fry that reviewers describe as a sharp, satisfying hit of heat. Don't skip the fried spring rolls with savoury and sweet fillings. Abalone in red sauce and crispy pork with cabbage are reliably reorder-worthy. The strength is the freshness of the seafood and a steady, experienced Chinese-style hand in the kitchen.

Price is accessible — averaging around 150 THB per head upward depending on how much seafood you order. Many say the value matches the quality. The atmosphere is informal, old-shophouse style — no air-con, slightly warm in the middle of the day. Worth knowing before going: the shop is small with no in-lane parking. Park outside and walk in. Late evenings and weekends see long queues; calling ahead to book is the safe move.

Open daily 11:00–20:00, with Google review scores around 4.2 stars from over a thousand reviewers. Reputation built over decades of word-of-mouth. If you want old-style Thai-Chinese cooking done with experience, Nai Roo is worth pinning on the Hat Yai map.
blocks.bestFor: Dinner with family or friends — order many dishes and share
blocks.spice: Medium to spicy (yam / spicy seafood stir-fries — adjustable)

blocks.title: Good to know before eating in Songkhla

items.title: Getting around
items.text: Nang Ngam Road in the Songkhla old town is walkable — great for eating and strolling. But between the old town of Songkhla, Hat Yai, and Ko Yo, distances are significant. Grab or a rental car is the most flexible option, especially for Ko Yo seafood outside the city.

items.title: Payments
items.text: Street spots and old institutions like stew rice, clay-pot ice cream, and bao shops mostly take cash. Keep small bills handy. Larger sit-down restaurants usually accept PromptPay transfer or card.

items.title: Timing and avoiding queues
items.text: Morning spots like Kiad Fang and Chok Dee Tae Tiam sell out early and queue long — arriving before 9am is the comfortable window. Ko Yo seafood on weekend evenings fills up; budget some time for waiting.

items.title: Language and menus
items.text: Many local restaurants have Thai-only menus, but staff at most places have seen tourists before. Point at the dish names from this article on your phone and you'll get what you want. Some Hat Yai restaurants have photo menus that make ordering easier.

items.title: Tipping
items.text: No tipping expected at street food or breakfast spots. At sit-down table-service restaurants, a small tip or rounding up the change is a nice gesture — not expected.

items.title: Spice levels
items.text: Southern Thai food and yam dishes at spots like Nai Roo or Long Oey are genuinely spicy. Ask for less chilli if you need to. Stew rice and dim sum are mild and approachable for everyone.

blocks.title: How to plan a full eating trip in Songkhla
blocks.html:
With limited time, split your days clearly for the best results. Start in the old town on Nang Ngam Road: eat Kiad Fang stew rice with a large bao while the shop is still quiet (it opens early and sells out fast), then walk off the meal in the old town before closing with a cup of clay-pot ice cream — it's on the same road. Lunch could be Tae Hiang Io for yam mamuang and sea bass sour curry.

Save Hat Yai for another day. Wake up early for Chok Dee Tae Tiam — queue for dim sum and ba kut teh from the morning session. Pick up Go Auan Baozi original fried bao to take with you. Then in the evening drive out to Ko Yo and have seafood at Nam Kiang Din with the lagoon view. For dinner back in Hat Yai, choose between Long Oey or Nai Roo depending on your mood.

faq.q: Which restaurant in this list is the most famous?
faq.a: Kiad Fang stew rice on Nang Ngam Road is the most talked-about — an institution that has been part of Songkhla for nearly nine decades and whose stew rice was named the provincial heritage dish. On the Hat Yai side, Chok Dee Tae Tiam is the dim sum and ba kut teh shop where queues form at dawn every day.

faq.q: What are Songkhla's signature dishes to try?
faq.a: Pork stew rice with dark spiced broth and a large bao at Kiad Fang; generous dim sum and ba kut teh at Chok Dee Tae Tiam; original fried bao at Go Auan; fresh seafood like grilled sweet clams and squid with roe at Nam Kiang Din on Ko Yo; and the old-style clay-pot ice cream with salted egg and Milo on Nang Ngam Road.

faq.q: How much does eating in Songkhla cost per person?
faq.a: Snacks like Go Auan bao are 18–35 THB each; a cup of clay-pot ice cream is 20–35 THB. Stew rice and dim sum restaurants run about 100–250 THB per person. Seafood at Nam Kiang Din on Ko Yo and Thai restaurants like Long Oey go higher at around 200–500 THB per person depending on what you order.

faq.q: Do restaurants here require advance booking?
faq.a: Street spots and morning restaurants like Kiad Fang, Chok Dee Tae Tiam, and the clay-pot ice cream shop don't require reservations — just come early because queues form and items sell out fast. For sit-down dinner spots like Nam Kiang Din on Ko Yo, Long Oey, or Tae Hiang Io, calling ahead for a table on weekends or with a large group is a good idea.

faq.q: Which spots are open in the evenings or late at night?
faq.a: Long Oey in Hat Yai opens from evening onward and runs until midnight — a good dinner destination. Nam Kiang Din on Ko Yo is open until around 22:00, perfect for a lagoon-view evening meal. Nai Roo and Tae Hiang Io focus on lunch-to-early-evening. Stew rice and Chok Dee Tae Tiam are morning spots that close in the afternoon.
